snip.t: Characterised by caseating or necrotising granulomas in affected organs
snip.s: Internal Medicine Respiratory CAT 1: 30 MCQs and 5 short answer questions

snip.t: Sarcoidosis: non-caseating granulomas; young adults; bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with or without parenchymal disease; erythema nodosum, arthralgia, uveitis, hypercalcaemia, raised ACE; Löfgren syndrome (bilateral hilar nodes + erythema nodosum + arthralgia, good prognosis).
Sarcoid: bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy; non-caseating granulomas.

Immune complex formation in the interstitium – Th1‑mediated granulomatous response: Organic antigens (mould spores, bird proteins) trigger type III/IV hypersensitivity → hypersensitivity pneumonitis with lymphocytic alveolitis, granulomas, and eventual fibrosis.
Berylliosis: Beryllium — Aerospace, electronics, nuclear — Granulomas that look like sarcoid

| Benign lung nodule (hamartoma, granuloma) | Incidentally found solitary nodule, often calcified or fat‑containing | CT characteristics (popcorn calcification, fat density); stable size over 2 years; biopsy shows benign tissue |
Immune system: Macrophages (phagocytosis, granuloma formation), T-lymphocytes (cell-mediated immunity, cytokine production), granuloma structure (caseous necrosis, fibrous cuff).
| Sarcoidosis | Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, erythema nodosum, multi-system | Non-caseating granulomas on biopsy, elevated ACE |

qs.q: A 22-year-old woman presents with tender subcutaneous nodules on her shins and bilateral hilar adenopathy on chest radiography. A skin biopsy reveals non-caseating granulomas. This cell-mediated hypersensitivity reaction involves accumulation of which primary cell type?
o: Epithelioid macrophages together with activated T lymphocytes
Neutrophils combined directly with circulating immune complexes
Eosinophils recruited alongside IgE‑coated mucosal mast cells
Plasma cells proliferating alongside cytotoxic lymphocyte clones
Fibroblasts depositing a dense collagen‑rich extracellular matrix
qs.e: Sarcoidosis is characterized by non-caseating granulomas composed primarily of activated macrophages and CD4+ T helper cells.
qs.s: Weekly Pathology Exam - October 30, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A patient presents with a chronic pulmonary infection characterized by caseating granulomas on histology. What is the commonest cause of infectious granulomas?
qs.e: Tuberculosis is recognized as the most common cause of infectious granulomas worldwide. Fungal and viral infections can also cause granulomas, but tuberculosis remains the classic primary etiology.
qs.s: General Pathology Continuous Assessment July 2021 — CAT — General: MCQs

qs.q: Ocular larva migrans caused by Toxocara canis can lead to granuloma formation and which secondary ocular complication?
qs.e: Ocular larva migrans from Toxocara canis can cause a granuloma that leads to secondary strabismus. Glaucoma is not the typical direct consequence of this larval migration.
qs.s: Year 3 Medical Parasitology II — CAT: MCQs

qs.q: A 45-year-old man presents with chronic, progressive monoarticular arthritis of the hip joint, accompanied by night sweats and low-grade fever. Synovial biopsy shows caseating granulomas. What is the pathogenesis of joint destruction in this condition?
o: Synovium grows as a pannus over articular cartilage
Direct viral cytolysis of the affected chondrocytes
Precipitation of monosodium urate crystals in joint
Immune complex deposition inside synovial membrane
qs.e: In mycobacterial arthritis, mycobacterial seeding leads to confluent granulomas with caseous necrosis, and the synovium grows as a pannus over articular cartilage, causing bone erosion. Crystal precipitation characterizes gout rather than mycobacterial joint infection.
qs.s: Infectious Arthritis: Bacterial, TB & Viral Joint Infections: MCQs

qs.q: A young intravenous drug user develops acute respiratory distress and pulmonary hypertension. Lung biopsy reveals foreign material surrounded by giant cell granulomas within the pulmonary vasculature. What is the causative agent?
qs.e: Talc embolism occurs in intravenous drug abusers when injected talc leads to granulomas and pulmonary hypertension. Amniotic fluid embolism is an obstetric emergency rather than a consequence of IV drug abuse.

qs.q: A patient with a multisystem disease is found to have noncaseating granulomas and elevated serum ACE levels. Which underlying pathological condition is most likely?
qs.e: Sarcoidosis is a multisystem disease characterized by noncaseating granulomas and elevated serum ACE levels. Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis presents with usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) and end-stage 'honeycomb lung'.

qs.q: A pregnant woman presents with a rapidly growing, red, pedunculated lesion on her gingiva that bleeds easily. If this lesion is a pyogenic granuloma, what is the most likely treatment?
o: Radical excision of the underlying bone
Systemic antibiotic therapy for Bartonella henselae
Observation, as it will regress spontaneously by age 7
qs.e: Pyogenic granulomas are treated with curettage and cautery. They do not regress by age 7 (that is for juvenile hemangiomas) and are not caused by Bartonella in this context.

qs.q: When does cell-mediated immunity typically become activated to surround Mycobacterium tuberculosis and form a granuloma during primary infection?
qs.e: Cell-mediated immunity gets activated and surrounds the cells to form a granuloma at approximately 3 weeks. Shorter timeframes like 2 days do not match this immunological milestone.

es.q: A 35-year-old female presents with fatigue, cough, and erythema nodosum. Biopsy shows noncaseating granulomas. What is the likely diagnosis, what is the characteristic histological finding, and what is the underlying mechanism for hypercalcemia if present in this condition?
es.m: 1. **Likely Diagnosis:** The likely diagnosis is Sarcoidosis, given the clinical presentation of erythema nodosum (a skin sign of acute sarcoidosis) and the histological finding of noncaseating granulomas. 2. **Characteristic Histological Finding:** The hallmark histological feature of sarcoidosis is the presence of noncaseating granulomas in multiple organs. Diagnosis is typically one of exclusion, after ruling out other causes of granulomatous disease. 3. **Mechanism of Hypercalcemia:** If hypercalcemia is present in sarcoidosis, it is caused by active Vitamin D production by activated macrophages within the granulomas. These macrophages possess 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity, leading to unr

es.q: A 35-year-old female presents with chronic cough and skin lesions. Biopsy reveals noncaseating granulomas in multiple organs. What is the likely diagnosis, and what common skin sign and metabolic derangement (with its cause) are associated with this condition?
es.m: The likely diagnosis is Sarcoidosis. - It is characterized by noncaseating granulomas in multiple organs. - A common skin sign associated with acute sarcoidosis is Erythema nodosum. - Hypercalcemia is a metabolic derangement caused by active Vitamin D production by macrophages within the granulomas.
es.s: Respiratory System Pathology 1A — Practice Questions — Essay Questions

es.q: A 35-year-old patient presents with constitutional symptoms, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, and skin lesions (erythema nodosum). A biopsy reveals noncaseating granulomas. Explain the characteristic histological finding for this condition and describe the mechanism behind the hypercalcemia sometime
es.m: The characteristic histological finding for this condition (Sarcoidosis) is the presence of **noncaseating granulomas** in multiple organs. Hypercalcemia in sarcoidosis is caused by **active Vitamin D production by macrophages within the granulomas**. These activated macrophages convert 25-hydroxyvitamin D to its active form, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, leading to increased intestinal calcium absorption and subsequent hypercalcemia.
es.s: Respiratory System Pathology 1A — Practice Questions — Essay Questions

es.q: A 30-year-old female presents with constitutional symptoms, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on chest X-ray, and skin lesions. Her biopsy shows noncaseating granulomas. What is the likely diagnosis, what is the associated skin sign, and how does this condition lead to hypercalcemia?
es.m: The likely diagnosis is **Sarcoidosis**. The associated skin sign, particularly in acute sarcoidosis, is **Erythema nodosum**. Sarcoidosis leads to hypercalcemia because the macrophages within the noncaseating granulomas become metabolically active and produce **active Vitamin D** (1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol). This increased production of active Vitamin D leads to enhanced intestinal absorption of calcium and subsequent hypercalcemia.
es.s: Respiratory System Pathology 1A — Practice Questions — Essay Questions

ai.summary: A granuloma is a focal collection of inflammatory cells, predominantly activated macrophages (epithelioid cells), forming a distinct microscopic aggregate. It represents a form of chronic inflammation initiated to contain an offending agent that is difficult to eradicate.

sections.p: A granuloma is a focal collection of inflammatory cells, predominantly activated macrophages (epithelioid cells), forming a distinct microscopic aggregate. It represents a form of chronic inflammation initiated to contain an offending agent that is difficult to eradicate.

b: Epithelioid Histiocytes: Activated macrophages with abundant pink cytoplasm and indistinct cell borders, resembling epithelial cells.
Multinucleated Giant Cells: Formed by the fusion of macrophages (e.g., Langhans giant cells in TB, with peripheral nuclei, or Foreign Body giant cells with central disorganized nuclei).
Lymphocytes: Usually form a 'cuff' around the periphery.
Fibroblasts: May produce a peripheral rim of collagen (fibrosis) in older lesions.
Caseating Granulomas: Characterized by central 'cheese-like' necrosis (e.g., *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*).
Non-caseating Granulomas: Lack central necrosis (e.g., Sarcoidosis, Crohn’s disease, beryllium exposure).
Infections: Tuberculosis (classic acid-fast bacilli), Leprosy, Schistosomiasis, and deep fungal infections (Histoplasmosis).
Immune-Mediated: Sarcoidosis, Crohn’s disease.
Foreign Bodies: Sutures, silica, or talc.

Diagnostic Significance: The presence of granulomas narrows the differential diagnosis significantly, often requiring special stains (e.g., Ziehl-Neelsen) or cultures to identify the causative pathogen.
Caseous necrosis leading to tissue destruction and cavity formation in the lungs.
Compression of vital structures, such as the airway or spinal cord, by enlarging masses.
Systemic spread of infection (miliary spread) if the immune system fails to contain the pathogen.
Organ dysfunction, such as liver or kidney failure, due to extensive replacement of healthy tissue by granulomas.

sections.p: Management focuses on identifying the underlying inflammatory or infectious trigger to stop new granuloma formation while managing existing tissue damage and systemic inflammation.
b: Antibiotics or antifungals are used to eliminate infectious triggers like Mycobacterium tuberculosis or Histoplasma.
Corticosteroids are prescribed to reduce non-infectious inflammation in conditions like sarcoidosis by inhibiting macrophage activation.
Immunosuppressants such as methotrexate may be used if steroids are ineffective or cause severe side effects.
Surgical excision is reserved for localized granulomas causing mechanical obstruction or when malignancy cannot be ruled out.
Refer to a specialist if there is vision loss, cardiac involvement, or progressive respiratory failure.
Serial imaging, such as chest X-rays, to monitor the size and stability of granulomatous lesions.
Screening of close contacts if the cause is identified as a contagious infection like tuberculosis.
Regular blood tests to monitor organ function and side effects of long-term immunosuppressant therapy.
Environmental modification to avoid exposure to known triggers like silica dust, bird droppings, or mold.
Granulation tissue: Consists of new capillaries and fibroblasts for wound healing, whereas granulomas are specific chronic inflammatory aggregates.
Abscesses: Characterized by acute neutrophilic infiltration and liquefactive necrosis rather than organized macrophage clusters.
Tumor metastases: Can mimic the nodular appearance of granulomas on imaging; biopsy is required to distinguish malignant cells from inflammatory cells.
Sputum smears: May be negative in pulmonary tuberculosis despite granuloma presence if the bacterial load is low or the lesion is closed.
ACE levels: Often elevated in sarcoidosis but lack specificity as they can rise in other granulomatous diseases like leprosy.
Chest X-ray: Hilar lymphadenopathy can appear identical in sarcoidosis, lymphoma, or fungal infections, requiring histological confirmation.

whenToSeekHelp: Persistent unexplained cough or coughing up blood.
Unintentional significant weight loss and drenching night sweats.
Rapidly enlarging, painless firm lumps in the neck or axilla.
Shortness of breath that worsens over a short period.

faq.a: A collection of epithelioid macrophages surrounded by a rim of lymphocytes and occasionally multinucleated giant cells, representing a type IV hypersensitivity response.

faq.q: What is the difference between caseating and non-caseating granulomas?
faq.a: Caseating granulomas have a central zone of 'cheese-like' necrosis typical of tuberculosis, while non-caseating granulomas lack central necrosis, common in sarcoidosis.

faq.q: What role do Langhans giant cells play?
faq.a: They are formed by the fusion of epithelioid macrophages with nuclei arranged in a horseshoe pattern at the periphery, characteristic of granulomatous inflammation.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused history and systematic exam can narrow the differential between infectious, immune and foreign‑body granulomas and identify complications such as airway obstruction, organ dysfunction or systemic spread.
b: Onset and duration of symptoms – acute (<2 weeks), sub‑acute (2 weeks–3 months) or chronic (>3 months).
Exposure history – travel, occupational dusts (silica, beryllium), animal contact, drug use, tattoos, sutures or implants.
Systemic features – fever, night sweats, weight loss, fatigue, arthralgia, erythema nodosum, ocular or neurologic symptoms.
Pulmonary specific – cough, hemoptysis, dyspnoea, chest pain, wheeze, history of TB exposure or HIV status.
Skin or mucosal lesions – nodules, papules, ulceration, gingival growth, location and tenderness.
Joint involvement – mono‑articular vs poly‑articular, swelling, range of motion, night pain.
Pregnancy or immunosuppression – HIV, steroids, diabetes, malnutrition.

t.b: Detects swelling, erythema, nodules or deformity; a positive finding suggests local granulomatous inflammation but cannot differentiate cause.
Tender, firm nodules favour infectious or foreign‑body granulomas; non‑tender, rubbery lesions are typical of sarcoid.

t.a: Percussion for dullness over lung fields
t.b: Dullness indicates consolidation or large granulomatous mass; cannot distinguish caseating from non‑caseating lesions.
Crackles suggest parenchymal involvement; wheeze may indicate airway compression by granuloma.
Limited motion with pain at night points to tuberculous arthritis; painless restriction suggests sarcoid.
Detects uveitis or chorioretinal granulomas; a positive result supports sarcoidosis or ocular toxocariasis.
Firm, non‑tender nodes with overlying skin changes raise suspicion for TB; soft, mobile nodes are less specific.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Select investigations that answer a specific clinical question; interpret results using validated cut‑offs and know alternatives when resources are limited.
b: Chest X‑ray – looks for hilar adenopathy, cavitation, nodular infiltrates; bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy favours sarcoid, cavitation suggests TB.
Sputum microscopy/culture for AFB – confirms mycobacterial infection; positive smear = active TB, negative does not exclude paucibacillary disease.
Serum ACE – screens for sarcoidosis; > 60 U/L supports diagnosis but is not definitive.
Serum calcium – hypercalcaemia (> 2.6 mmol/L) indicates active sarcoid granuloma conversion of vitamin D.
Tuberculin skin test (Mantoux) – induration ≥ 10 mm in high‑risk groups (HIV+, recent contact, immunosuppressed) suggests TB exposure.
IGRA (Quantiferon) – alternative to Mantoux; positive result indicates TB infection, not active disease.
Biopsy with histology – gold standard; caseating necrosis = TB/fungal, non‑caseating = sarcoid/immune, foreign‑body giant cells = exogenous material.
Fungal stains (Gomori methenamine silver) – detect deep fungal elements; negative does not rule out early infection.
Serology for HIV – CD4 count guides TB‑HIV co‑management; CD4 < 50 cells/µL requires early ART within 2 weeks of TB therapy.
Full blood count and ESR – inflammatory marker; marked eosinophilia may point to parasitic or drug‑induced granulomas.

t.b: Answers: presence and pattern of pulmonary granulomas. Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy → sarcoid; upper‑lobe cavitation → TB. If unavailable, use portable ultrasound for pleural effusion.
Answers: active mycobacterial infection. Positive smear = TB; culture gives species and drug susceptibility. If microscopy unavailable, send sputum for GeneXpert MTB/RIF.
Answers: likelihood of sarcoidosis. Value > 60 U/L supports diagnosis; normal value does not exclude it. If assay unavailable, rely on clinical and radiologic criteria.
Answers: granuloma‑mediated hypercalcaemia. > 2.6 mmol/L indicates active sarcoid; treat with hydration and steroids. If calcium not measurable, monitor symptoms of hypercalcaemia.
Answers: TB exposure in high‑risk groups. Induration ≥ 10 mm in HIV+, recent contacts, immunosuppressed = positive. In low‑risk adults, ≥ 15 mm is positive. If unavailable, use IGRA.
Answers: latent or active TB infection, not affected by BCG. Positive = TB infection; negative makes TB unlikely. If not affordable, rely on clinical risk assessment.

Answers: definitive histology and aetiology. Caseating necrosis + AFB = TB; non‑caseating granulomas + negative stains = sarcoid; foreign‑material giant cells = foreign‑body granuloma. If tissue unavailable, treat empirically based on most likely cause.
Answers: immunosuppression level. CD4 < 50 cells/µL → start ART within 2 weeks of TB therapy. If CD4 not measurable, start ART after 2 weeks of TB treatment.

sections.p: Combine clinical, radiologic and histologic data to assign a working diagnosis, stage pulmonary sarcoidosis, and grade severity for management decisions.
b: Sarcoidosis – non‑caseating granulomas, bilateral hilar adenopathy, serum ACE > 60 U/L, hypercalcaemia > 2.6 mmol/L; stage I (adenopathy only), II (adenopathy + infiltrates), III (infiltrates only), IV (fibrosis).
Tuberculous granuloma – caseating necrosis, positive AFB smear/culture or GeneXpert, compatible chest X‑ray (upper‑lobe cavitation), Mantoux ≥ 10 mm in high‑risk groups.
Fungal granuloma – caseating or non‑caseating granulomas with fungal hyphae on special stains; endemic exposure (e.g., Histoplasma capsulatum) and positive culture.
Foreign‑body granuloma – granulomas surrounding identifiable exogenous material on histology; history of trauma, injection, or inhaled particles.
Severity grading – based on organ involvement (lung > 50 % involvement, cardiac, ocular, neurologic), serum calcium, ACE trend, and functional impairment (e.g., FEV1 < 50 % predicted).
Staging for extrapulmonary disease – use organ‑specific scoring (e.g., cardiac MRI for sarcoid myocarditis, ophthalmic exam for uveitis).

sections.p: Granulomatous inflammation can mimic several other pathologies; a systematic comparison helps avoid misdiagnosis.

t.b: Points to infection: fever, night sweats, positive AFB/fungal stains, caseation. Points to sarcoid: asymptomatic, bilateral hilar adenopathy, ACE > 60 U/L, non‑caseating granulomas. Separate by microbiology and stains.

Points to foreign body: history of trauma or inhaled particles, giant cells with visible material, minimal systemic symptoms. Immune granuloma: systemic signs, no identifiable material, often non‑caseating. Separate by histology.

Points to vasculitis: necrotizing granulomas with vasculitis, ANCA positivity, upper airway involvement. Infection: organism detection, caseation, positive cultures. Separate by serology and microbiology.

t.a: Lymphoma with granulomatous reaction vs. true granuloma
t.b: Points to lymphoma: rapid node enlargement, B‑symptoms, atypical cells on biopsy, flow cytometry positive. Granuloma: organized epithelioid cells, no malignant cells. Separate by immunophenotyping.

sections.p: A pragmatic ladder for granulomatous disease that works in low‑resource hospitals, from stabilising the patient to definitive therapy and safe escalation.
b: 1. Stabilise: assess airway, breathing, circulation; treat fever, pain and hypoxia; obtain basic labs (CBC, ESR/CRP, renal & liver function, calcium).
2. Identify a treatable trigger: send tissue for Ziehl‑Neelsen, PAS, fungal culture, and PCR if available; order chest X‑ray/ultrasound for organ involvement.
3. Empiric anti‑infective therapy when TB or deep fungal infection is likely (e.g., rifampicin‑based regimen, itraconazole) while awaiting results.
4. Initiate disease‑specific therapy: corticosteroids for immune granulomas (sarcoidosis, Crohn’s) after infection excluded; methotrexate or azathioprine if steroids contraindicated or need sparing.
5. Monitor response: clinical improvement, repeat imaging at 2‑4 weeks, track inflammatory markers and calcium; adjust therapy if no response.
6. Escalate or refer: worsening organ function, uncontrolled hypercalcaemia, large airway obstruction, spinal cord compression, or diagnostic uncertainty → refer to specialist centre.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Key adverse effects of the main drug classes used for granulomatous disease and practical actions for each.
b: Corticosteroids – hyperglycaemia, hypertension, infection risk, osteoporosis; monitor glucose, blood pressure, give calcium/vitamin D, treat opportunistic infections promptly.

Rifampicin – hepatotoxicity, drug‑induced orange fluids, induces CYP enzymes reducing levels of oral contraceptives and antiretrovirals; check LFTs monthly, advise contraception change, adjust ART doses.
Itraconazole – hepatotoxicity, heart failure risk, strong CYP3A4 inhibition; obtain baseline LFTs, avoid in decompensated heart failure, watch for drug interactions (e.g., statins).
Methotrexate – bone‑marrow suppression, hepatic fibrosis, pulmonary toxicity; monitor CBC and LFTs every 4 weeks, supplement folic acid, stop if dyspnoea or rising transaminases.
Azathioprine – myelosuppression, hepatotoxicity, TPMT deficiency risk; test TPMT activity if possible, monitor CBC/LFTs, reduce dose if counts fall.

sections.p: Potential complications of granulomatous disease and clear triggers for urgent escalation or specialist referral.
b: Progressive organ dysfunction – rising creatinine, worsening liver enzymes, or declining pulmonary function; refer for organ‑specific specialist.
Hypercalcaemia >2.6 mmol/L with neuro‑cognitive symptoms or renal stones; start steroids, hydrate, consider bisphosphonates, refer if refractory.
Mass effect – airway obstruction, spinal cord compression, or large intra‑abdominal masses causing obstruction; arrange urgent imaging and surgical consultation.
Severe infection secondary to immunosuppression – fever, new infiltrates, sepsis; broaden antimicrobial coverage, stop or taper immunosuppressants, admit to higher‑level care.
Drug toxicity requiring cessation – transaminases >5 × ULN, neuropathy, cytopenias; stop offending agent, switch to alternative, involve pharmacy.

sections.p: How common co‑morbidities and contextual factors modify presentation, investigations and treatment of granulomas.
b: HIV – blunted tuberculin response, higher risk of disseminated TB; use GeneXpert if available, start ART after 2 weeks if CD4 < 50 cells/µL, avoid steroids unless life‑threatening inflammation.
Malnutrition – low albumin reduces drug binding, increases toxicity; give nutritional support, adjust dosing for weight, monitor for electrolyte disturbances.
Diabetes – steroids worsen glycaemia; intensify insulin or oral agents, check glucose daily, consider steroid‑sparing agents.
Alcohol use – potentiates hepatotoxicity of isoniazid, rifampicin, azathioprine; counsel cessation, monitor LFTs closely.
Renal failure – dose‑adjust drugs cleared renally (e.g., ethambutol, methotrexate); use therapeutic drug monitoring where possible.
Liver failure – avoid hepatotoxic agents; prefer steroids alone or non‑hepatotoxic antifungals, monitor bilirubin and INR.
Age extremes – children need weight‑based dosing, elderly have reduced hepatic clearance; start low, titrate slowly, watch for delirium.

sections.p: Tailored considerations for children, pregnant women, the elderly, people with HIV and settings with limited resources.
b: Children – obtain tissue when possible, use pediatric TB regimen (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol), avoid methotrexate, use age‑appropriate steroid dosing, monitor growth.
Pregnancy – prioritize safety: steroids for sarcoidosis, ethambutol‑based TB therapy, avoid teratogenic immunosuppressants, schedule delivery after disease control.
Elderly – start steroids at low dose, watch for osteoporosis, delirium, and renal impairment; consider steroid‑sparing agents only if benefits outweigh risks.
People with HIV – screen for TB with GeneXpert, start ART according to CD4 count, use rifabutin if on protease inhibitors, treat opportunistic infections before heavy immunosuppression.

Low‑resource settings – rely on clinical algorithms, use sputum smear and chest X‑ray when culture unavailable, treat presumptive TB with standard 6‑month regimen, use oral prednisolone for sarcoidosis, arrange referral for surgical complications.

facts: Granuloma formation requires IFN‑γ and TNF‑α activation of macrophages
Caseating granulomas show central necrosis; non‑caseating lack necrosis
Serum calcium > 2.6 mmol/L indicates hypercalcaemia in sarcoidosis
Mantoux induration ≥10 mm for HIV‑positive or recent TB contact
RIPE therapy (Rifampicin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol) for TB granulomas
Start ART within 2 weeks of TB treatment if CD4 <50 cells/µL
Langhans giant cells have peripheral nuclei arranged horseshoe‑shaped
Erythema nodosum is a common extra‑pulmonary sign of sarcoidosis
Biopsy of sarcoid granuloma shows tight, non‑necrotic epithelioid cell clusters with scant lymphocytes

vivas.q: What cytokines are essential for granuloma maintenance?
vivas.a: IFN‑γ activates macrophages; TNF‑α maintains granuloma architecture and prevents dissemination

vivas.q: How do you differentiate a foreign‑body granuloma from an immune granuloma histologically?
vivas.a: Foreign‑body granulomas have multinucleated giant cells surrounding inert material, little lymphocyte cuff; immune granulomas have epithelioid cells, Langhans giant cells, and a lymphocyte rim

vivas.q: A patient with bilateral hilar adenopathy, erythema nodosum and non‑caseating granulomas – what is the most likely diagnosis?
vivas.a: Sarcoidosis

vivas.q: What is the first‑line drug regimen for TB granulomas?
vivas.a: RIPE (Rifampicin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol) for 2 months then continuation phase

vivas.q: When should ART be started in an HIV‑TB co‑infected patient with CD4 30 cells/µL?
vivas.a: Within 2 weeks of initiating TB therapy

vivas.q: Explain why steroids are avoided in caseating granulomas due to infection.
vivas.a: Steroids suppress immune containment, risking spread of the pathogen; they are reserved for non‑infectious granulomas

vivas.q: What bedside test helps identify pulmonary granulomas?
vivas.a: Chest auscultation for crackles plus percussion for dullness; imaging is required for definitive diagnosis

vivas.q: How does a positive Mantoux test aid granuloma work‑up?
vivas.a: An induration ≥10 mm in high‑risk groups suggests TB infection, prompting sputum microscopy and possible biopsy

vivas.q: What is the significance of elevated serum ACE in granulomatous disease?
vivas.a: It reflects macrophage activation in sarcoidosis; values >60 U/L support the diagnosis but are not definitive

vivas.q: Describe the histological hallmark of sarcoid granuloma.
vivas.a: Tight, non‑necrotic epithelioid cell clusters with a thin peripheral lymphocyte rim and occasional asteroid bodies

vivas.q: Why can hypercalcaemia occur in sarcoidosis?
vivas.a: Activated macrophages express 1‑α‑hydroxylase, converting vitamin D to its active form, increasing calcium absorption

vivas.q: What is the next step after finding caseating granulomas on lung biopsy?
vivas.a: Obtain sputum for acid‑fast bacilli and start empirical TB therapy pending culture

vivas.q: How do you distinguish TB from histoplasmosis granulomas?
vivas.a: TB shows caseation and acid‑fast bacilli; histoplasmosis shows small yeasts within macrophages and may be non‑caseating

vivas.q: What complication can a large mediastinal granuloma cause?
vivas.a: Compression of the airway or great vessels leading to dyspnoea or superior vena cava syndrome

vivas.q: When is surgical excision indicated for granulomas?
vivas.a: When the lesion causes mechanical obstruction, persistent pain, or when malignancy cannot be excluded

vivas.q: A 22‑year‑old woman with tender shins nodules, hilar adenopathy, non‑caseating granulomas – what hypersensitivity type is this?
vivas.a: Type IV (cell‑mediated) hypersensitivity

vivas.q: What is the commonest infectious cause of caseating granulomas?
vivas.a: Mycobacterium tuberculosis

vivas.q: Toxocara canis ocular larva migrans can cause granuloma and which secondary ocular complication?
vivas.a: Retinal detachment

vivas.q: Pathogenesis of caseating granulomas in hip arthritis?
vivas.a: Hematogenous spread of Mycobacterium tuberculosis to synovium, triggering a Th1 response and granuloma formation

vivas.q: Causative agent of foreign‑material giant‑cell granulomas in pulmonary vasculature of IV drug users?
vivas.a: Micro‑emboli of injected talc or cellulose from adulterated drugs

mcqs.q: A 30‑year‑old man presents with chronic cough, weight loss, and chest X‑ray showing hilar lymphadenopathy. Biopsy shows non‑caseating granulomas. Which laboratory result best supports sarcoidosis?
mcqs.e: ACE >60 U/L is supportive of sarcoidosis

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical feature of a foreign‑body granuloma?
o: Multinucleated giant cells surrounding inert material
mcqs.e: Foreign‑body granulomas lack the peripheral lymphocyte cuff seen in immune granulomas

mcqs.q: In sarcoidosis, which radiographic pattern is most common?
mcqs.e: Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy is classic for sarcoidosis

mcqs.q: Which cytokine blockade is contraindicated in active TB granulomas?
mcqs.e: Anti‑TNF‑α can cause TB reactivation by disrupting granuloma maintenance

mcqs.q: A 45‑year‑old HIV‑positive patient with CD4 40 cells/µL is started on TB therapy. When should ART be initiated?
mcqs.e: Guidelines recommend ART within 2 weeks for CD4 <50 cells/µL

cases.v: A 28‑year‑old male farmer presents with 3 weeks of dry cough, low‑grade fever, and erythema nodosum on shins. Chest X‑ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Skin biopsy reveals tight, non‑caseating granulomas with asteroid bodies.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
Which serum test would support this diagnosis?

qs.a: Observation if asymptomatic; consider oral prednisone for organ‑threatening disease

cases.v: A 42‑year‑old woman with a history of IV drug use presents with acute dyspnoea and right‑sided chest pain. CT pulmonary angiography shows emboli with surrounding granulomatous reaction containing foreign material. Histology shows multinucleated giant cells around refractile particles.

qs.q: What is the likely causative material?
qs.a: Talc or cellulose adulterant in injected drugs
Stabilize airway, give anticoagulation for emboli, and consider surgical embolectomy if hemodynamically unstable
Steroids would suppress immune clearance of the foreign material and increase infection risk

mistakes: Confusing serum ACE cut‑off values; use a single consistent >60 U/L
Applying a universal Mantoux >10 mm cut‑off; adjust for risk group
Mixing mg/dL and mmol/L for calcium; keep >2.6 mmol/L for hypercalcaemia
Starting ART too early in TB with CD4 >50 cells/µL; wait 8 weeks unless severe disease
Prescribing steroids for caseating TB granulomas; they worsen infection
Assuming all granulomas are infectious; consider non‑infectious causes first
exam: What cytokines are essential for granuloma maintenance? — IFN‑γ activates macrophages; TNF‑α maintains granuloma architecture and prevents dissemination

How do you differentiate a foreign‑body granuloma from an immune granuloma histologically? — Foreign‑body granulomas have multinucleated giant cells surrounding inert material, little lymphocyte cuff; immune granulomas have epithelioid cells, Langhans giant cells, and a lymphocyte rim
A patient with bilateral hilar adenopathy, erythema nodosum and non‑caseating granulomas – what is the most likely diagnosis? — Sarcoidosis
What is the first‑line drug regimen for TB granulomas? — RIPE (Rifampicin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol) for 2 months then continuation phase
When should ART be started in an HIV‑TB co‑infected patient with CD4 30 cells/µL? — Within 2 weeks of initiating TB therapy
Explain why steroids are avoided in caseating granulomas due to infection. — Steroids suppress immune containment, risking spread of the pathogen; they are reserved for non‑infectious granulomas
What bedside test helps identify pulmonary granulomas? — Chest auscultation for crackles plus percussion for dullness; imaging is required for definitive diagnosis
How does a positive Mantoux test aid granuloma work‑up? — An induration ≥10 mm in high‑risk groups suggests TB infection, prompting sputum microscopy and possible biopsy
What is the significance of elevated serum ACE in granulomatous disease? — It reflects macrophage activation in sarcoidosis; values >60 U/L support the diagnosis but are not definitive
Describe the histological hallmark of sarcoid granuloma. — Tight, non‑necrotic epithelioid cell clusters with a thin peripheral lymphocyte rim and occasional asteroid bodies
Why can hypercalcaemia occur in sarcoidosis? — Activated macrophages express 1‑α‑hydroxylase, converting vitamin D to its active form, increasing calcium absorption
What is the next step after finding caseating granulomas on lung biopsy? — Obtain sputum for acid‑fast bacilli and start empirical TB therapy pending culture
How do you distinguish TB from histoplasmosis granulomas? — TB shows caseation and acid‑fast bacilli; histoplasmosis shows small yeasts within macrophages and may be non‑caseating
What complication can a large mediastinal granuloma cause? — Compression of the airway or great vessels leading to dyspnoea or superior vena cava syndrome
